title: Final Scene
text:
I have left the door ajar.

I am an animal that does not resign itself

to dying. Eternity

is the dark hinge that gives way,

a small noise in the night

of flesh.

I am the island that advances, sustained

by death, or a city

fiercely besieged

by life,

or perhaps I am nothing,

only insomnia

and the brilliant indifference of the stars, desert, inexorable destiny, the sun of the living rises, I recognize that door, there is no other, spring ice and a thorn of blood in the eye of the rose.
editorial_note: The translation preserves the ajar door, hinge of eternity, and the compressed final sentence of cosmic indifference.

title: In a Low Voice
text:
slowness is beauty

I copy these borrowed lines

I breathe

I accept the light

under the thin air of November

under the grass

without color

under the cracked

gray sky

I accept mourning and feast

I have not arrived

I will never arrive

at the center of everything

is the intact poem,

inescapable sun,

night without turning its head.

I prowl its light,

its animal shadow

of words,

I sniff its splendor,

its footprint,

its remains,

all to say

that once

I was attentive,

disarmed,


alone almost

in death,

almost in fire.
editorial_note: The translation keeps the low-voiced ars poetica of circling the intact poem without arriving.

title: So Be It
text:
The day remains behind,

barely consumed and already useless.

The great light begins,

all doors yield before a man

asleep,

time is a tree that never ceases growing.


Time,

the great door ajar,

the star that blinds.


It is not with the eyes that one sees born

that drop of light that will be,

that once was.


Sing, bee, without haste,

travel the illuminated labyrinth,

in celebration.


Breathe and sing.

Where everything ends, open your wings.

You are the sun,

the sting of dawn,

the sea that kisses the mountains,

total clarity,

the dream.
editorial_note: The translation preserves the liturgical motion from spent day to bee-song and opening wings.

title: Song Five
text:
Across the bridges of Zamora,

alone and slow, went my soul.


Not across the iron bridge;

the stone one was the one it loved.


At times it looked at the sky,

at times it looked at the water.


Across the bridges of Zamora,

alone and slow, went my soul.
editorial_note: The translation keeps the simple refrain and the preference for the stone bridge.

title: I Ask for Peace and the Word
text:
I write

in defense of the kingdom

of man and his justice. I ask

for peace

and the word. I have said

"silence,"

"shadow,"

"void,"

etcetera.

I say

"of man and his justice,"

"Pacific Ocean,"

what they let me.

I ask

for peace and the word.
editorial_note: The translation keeps Otero's public plea and the restrained inventory of permitted words.

title: In the Beginning
text:
If I have lost life, time, everything

I threw, like a ring, into the water,

if I have lost my voice in the thicket,

the word remains to me.


If I have suffered thirst, hunger, everything

that was mine and turned out to be nothing,

if I have reaped the shadows in silence,

the word remains to me.


If I opened my lips to see the pure

and terrible face of my homeland,

if I opened my lips until I tore them,

the word remains to me.
editorial_note: The translation preserves the repeated claim that after every loss, the word remains.

title: Woman's Body
text:
Woman's body, river of gold

where, arms sunk deep, we receive

a blue lightning flash, clusters

of light torn in a leafiness of gold.


Woman's body, or sea of gold,

where, loving with our hands, we do not know

whether the breasts are waves, whether the arms

are oars, whether they are only wings of gold...


Woman's body, fountain of weeping

where, after so much light, so much

subtle touch, Tantalus' pain remains.


The solitude of God sounds. We feel

the solitude of two. And a chain

that does not sound anchors souls and mud in God.
editorial_note: The translation keeps the erotic-gold imagery as it turns toward divine solitude and the silent chain.

title: Mademoiselle Isabel
text:
Mademoiselle Isabel, blond and French,

with a blackbird beneath your skin,

I do not know if that one or this one, oh mademoiselle

Isabel, sings in him or if he sings in that one.

Princess of my childhood; you, princess,

promise, with two carnation breasts;

I,

le livre,

le crayon,

le

...

le

..., oh Isabel,

Isabel..., your garden trembles on the table.

At night, you smoothed your hair,

I fell asleep, meditating on it

and on your rose body: butterfly,

pink and white, veiled with a veil.

Flown forever from my rose

—mademoiselle Isabel— and from my sky.
editorial_note: The translation keeps the French fragments and childhood-erotic memory of Isabel.

title: Enough
text:
For a moment I imagined my horror:

that God, the only living one, did not exist,

or that, existing, he consisted only

of earth, of water, of fire, of shadow, of wind.


And that death, oh shudder,

were the lightless hollow of a stairway,

a colossal void sinking

into a desolate, slimy silence.


Then why live, oh sons

of mother, toward what stained glass, crucifixes

and all the rest? Death is enough.


Enough. Finish, oh God, mistreating us.

Or else, let us hurl ourselves

upon You—hoarse river that returns.
editorial_note: The translation preserves the sonnet's theological horror and its final demand to God.

title: I Say Living
text:
Because living has become red-hot.

(Blood was always red, oh God.)

I say living, living as if nothing

were to remain of what I write.


Because writing is fugitive wind,

and publishing, a column pushed into a corner.

I say living, living by pulse, angrily

dying, calling from the stirrup.


I return to life with my death on my shoulder,

abominating all I have written: rubble

of that man I was when I kept silent.


Now I return to my being, go back to my

most immortal work: that fierce festival

of living and dying. The rest is surplus.
editorial_note: The translation keeps the red-hot urgency and the turn from writing toward living-and-dying as the true work.
